topic: Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues, and Eigenbasis: The Geometry of Linear Transformations

sections.title: Intuitive Hook: The 'Stretch' Concept
sections.content: Introduce linear transformation as a visual deformation of a 2D grid. Most vectors change direction when a matrix acts on them. We identify the 'special' vectors that remain on their original span—only scaled.
sections.example: Imagine a logo on a rubber sheet; when you stretch the sheet, most points shift diagonally, but points along the axis of the stretch stay on that line.

sections.title: Defining Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
sections.content: Formalize the equation Av = λv. Define 'Eigenvector' (v) as the direction that doesn't change, and 'Eigenvalue' (λ) as the factor by which it is stretched or squashed. Use a visual animation where v stays locked on a line.
sections.example: If matrix A represents a transformation, and v is an eigenvector with λ=2, the vector v simply doubles in length.

sections.title: Visualizing Eigenbasis
sections.content: Explain that an Eigenbasis is a set of eigenvectors that act as a 'special coordinate system.' In this basis, the complex transformation matrix A becomes a simple diagonal matrix, making calculations much faster.
sections.example: Switching from standard (x, y) coordinates to (v1, v2) coordinates is like rotating your camera to align with the stretch of the rubber sheet, making the transformation look like simple scaling.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The 'Search Engine' Perspective
sections.content: Briefly connect the abstract math to practical utility. Explain how identifying the most significant eigenvalues helps in simplifying data (dimensionality reduction/PCA).
sections.example: Think of a social network: the 'principal eigenvector' of a connection matrix identifies the most influential people (PageRank) based on how their influence scales across the network.

sections.title: Summary and Synthesis
sections.content: Recap: A matrix is just a function. Eigenvectors are the 'invariant axes' of that function, and eigenvalues tell us the 'intensity' of the transformation along those axes.
sections.example: A quick visual animation: A square grid transforming into a rectangle, highlighting the two eigenvectors remaining fixed as the grid scales.
